formulations.note: Two UK SmPCs for 40 mg tablets were used. They differ in some wording (indications, children under 12, pregnancy and breastfeeding); differences are shown per source.

src.q: Each tablet contains 40mg Furosemide.
Each tablet contains 40 mg of furosemide as the active substance.

items.t: Oedema with congestive heart failure, liver cirrhosis or renal disease (including nephrotic syndrome); peripheral oedema due to mild to moderate hypertension.

restrictions.note: No prescribing restrictions stated in the UK SmPCs.

items.t: Adults and children over 12: initially 40 mg in the morning; maintenance 20 mg daily or 40 mg on alternate days; up to 80 mg daily in resistant oedema.

src.q: Initially 40mg daily in the morning
Maintenance dose is 20mg daily or 40mg on alternate days, increased in resistant oedema to 80mg daily.

items.t: 20-40 mg twice daily. If 40 mg twice daily is not enough, add another antihypertensive rather than increasing the dose.

src.q: Hypertension: 20-40mg twice daily; if 40mg twice daily does not lead to a clinically satisfactory response, the addition of other antihypertensive agents, rather than an increase in the dose of furosemide should be considered.

items.t: One UK SmPC (chronic renal insufficiency): 250 mg daily initially, increased in 250 mg steps every 4-6 hours to a maximum of 1,500 mg in 24 hours (exceptionally 2,000 mg). This conflicts with the same SmPC's contraindication when creatinine clearance is below 30 mL/min per 1.73 m²; the SmPC does not resolve this.

src.q: In patients with chronic renal insufficiency, an initial daily dose of 250mg is employed.
up to a maximum daily dose of 1,500mg in 24 hours. In exceptional cases up to 2,000mg in 24 hours may be given.

items.t: Elderly: eliminated more slowly; titrate to response. Dose changes may be needed in hypoproteinaemia or liver congestion/dysfunction.

src.q: Elderly: Generally eliminated more slowly. Dosage should be titrated until the required response is achieved.

Children under 12 years : A more suitable dosage form should be used in this age group.

items.t: Premature infants: risk of nephrocalcinosis/nephrolithiasis (renal function must be monitored and renal ultrasound performed) and of persistent patent ductus arteriosus.

src.q: In premature infants there is a risk of development of nephrocalcinosis/nephrolithiasis.
In premature infants with respiratory distress syndrome, administration of furosemide tablets in the initial weeks after birth entails an increased risk of a persistent patent ductus arteriosus.
Renal function must be monitored and renal ultrasonography performed

items.t: Correct hypotension, hypovolaemia and acid-base disturbance before starting. Symptomatic hypotension (dizziness, fainting) is more likely in the elderly and with other blood-pressure-lowering medicines.

src.q: These and any acid-base disturbance should be corrected before furosemide is started.
Symptomatic hypotension leading to dizziness, fainting or loss of consciousness can occur in patients treated with furosemide, particularly in the elderly

items.t: Caution in impaired hepatic or renal function, hepatorenal syndrome, diabetes (latent diabetes may appear; insulin needs may rise), the elderly, urinary outflow obstruction including prostatic hypertrophy (acute retention), gout, and those at risk from marked falls in blood pressure. Stop before a glucose tolerance test.

src.q: Diabetes mellitus (latent diabetes may become overt: insulin requirements in established diabetes may increase)

items.t: Hypoproteinaemia (e.g. nephrotic syndrome): careful dose titration (reduced effect, more ototoxicity).

src.q: Patients with hypoproteinaemia (such as that associated with the nephrotic syndrome) require careful dose titration (reduced furosemide effect: increased risk of ototoxicity)

items.t: Lactose: patients with galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.

items.t: Sulfonamide allergy (SPS): loop diuretics are non-antibiotic sulfonamides; cross-reactivity with sulfonamide antibiotics is not expected, but the SmPC lists sulphonamide hypersensitivity as a contraindication.

src.q: Classes where all members have a sulfonamide group include: carbonic anhydrase inhibitors loop diuretics
Cross-reactivity between antibiotic and non-antibiotic sulfonamides is not expected, including in people who had a life-threatening reaction to a sulfonamide.

items.t: ACE inhibitors: marked fall in blood pressure and worse renal function. Reduce the furosemide dose for at least 3 days, or stop it, before starting or increasing an ACE inhibitor.

src.q: A marked fall in blood pressure and deterioration in renal function may be seen when ACE inhibitors are added to furosemide therapy.
The dose of furosemide should be reduced for at least three days, or the drug stopped, before initiating the ACE inhibitor or increasing the dose of an ACE inhibitor.
Furosemide should be stopped or the dose reduced before starting an ACE-inhibitor.

items.t: Potassium supplements and potassium-sparing diuretics: contraindicated in section 4.3 (one SmPC notes increased hyperkalaemia risk with potassium salts).

src.q: Concomitant potassium supplements or potassium-sparing diuretics
Potassium salts: There is an increased risk of hyperkalaemia when given with potassium salts.

items.t: Aminoglycosides, polymyxins, vancomycin: more ototoxicity (may be irreversible); use only if there are compelling medical reasons. Aminoglycosides and some high-dose cephalosporins: more nephrotoxicity.

src.q: There is an increased risk of ototoxicity when loop diuretics are given with aminoglycosides, polymyxins or vancomycin. Since this may lead to irreversible damage, these drugs must only be used with furosemide if there are compelling medical reasons.
Impairment of renal function may develop in patients receiving concurrent treatment with furosemide and high doses of certain cephalosporins.

items.t: NSAIDs: more nephrotoxicity and reduced diuretic effect; acute renal insufficiency if dehydrated. Salicylate toxicity may be increased.

src.q: NSAIDs - increased risk of nephrotoxicity (especially if there is hypovolaemia).
In patients with dehydration or hypovolaemia, NSAIDs may cause acute renal insufficiency.
Salicylic toxicity may be increased by furosemide.

items.t: Lithium: reduced lithium excretion and toxicity risk; avoid unless plasma lithium levels are monitored (one SmPC); monitor lithium levels carefully and adjust the lithium dose where necessary (another SmPC).

src.q: Avoid concomitant administration unless plasma levels are monitored.
Lithium: Loop diuretics reduce the excretion of lithium
it is recommended that lithium levels are carefully monitored and where necessary the lithium dosage is adjusted

items.t: Hypokalaemia (and hypomagnesaemia) increases cardiac toxicity with QT-prolonging drugs, antiarrhythmics and cardiac glycosides; avoid with pimozide. Extra hypokalaemia with thiazides, corticosteroids and high-dose beta2 agonists (e.g. salbutamol).

src.q: Drugs associated with QT prolongation - cardiac toxicity may be increased by furosemide-induced hypokalaemia and/or hypomagnesaemia.
There is an increased risk of hypokalaemia when loop diuretics are given with thiazides and related diuretics.
There is an increased risk of hypokalaemia when loop diuretics are given with corticosteroids.
Anti-arrhythmics (including amiodarone, disopyramide, flecainide and sotalol) - risk of cardiac toxicity (because of furosemide-induced hypokalaemia).
Cardiac glycosides - hypokalaemia and electrolyte disturbances (including magnesium) increases the risk of cardiac toxicity.
Avoid concurrent use with pimozide.
Sympathomimetics - increased risk of hypokalaemia with high doses of beta2 sympathomimetics

items.t: Other: enhanced hypotension with other antihypertensives, nitrates, alpha-blockers (first-dose effect), tricyclics (postural); antidiabetic effect antagonised; carbamazepine (hyponatraemia); oestrogens and progestogens antagonise the diuretic effect; laxative abuse adds to potassium loss; one SmPC says antihistamines add hypokalaemia-related cardiac toxicity; sucralfate and bile acid sequestrants reduce absorption (separate doses); methotrexate and probenecid (mutual renal-secretion effects); warfarin (albumin binding in low albumin).

src.q: Antidiabetics - hypoglycaemic effects antagonised by furosemide.
Furosemide and sucralfate must not be taken within 2 hours of each other
Conversely, furosemide may decrease renal elimination of these drugs.
Antihypertensives - enhanced hypotensive effect possible with all types.
Nitrates - enhanced hypotensive effect.
There is a risk of a first-dose effect with post-synaptic alpha blockers e.g. prazosin.
Increased risk of postural hypotension with TCAs (tricyclic antidepressants).
Antiepileptics - increased risk of hyponatraemia with carbamazepine.
Oestrogens and progestogens - diuretic effect antagonized.
Laxative abuse - increases the risk of potassium loss.
Antihistamines - hypokalaemia with increased risk of cardiac toxicity.
Bile acid sequestrants (e.g. colestyramine: colestipol) - reduced absorption of furosemide - administer 2 to 3 hours apart.
Probenecid, methotrexate and other drugs which, like furosemide, undergo significant renal tubular secretion may reduce the effect of furosemide.
Warfarin and clofibrate compete with furosemide in the binding to serum albumin.

items.t: Contraindicated in anuria and when creatinine clearance is below 30 mL/min per 1.73 m² (both UK SmPCs), and in renal failure caused by nephrotoxic or hepatotoxic poisoning.

src.q: In patients with chronic renal insufficiency, an initial daily dose of 250mg is employed.

items.t: SPS: if creatinine rises 30-50%, exceeds 200 micromol/L, or eGFR falls below 30 mL/min/1.73 m², review volume status promptly, reduce or stop if hypovolaemic, and recheck within 1 week. If creatinine rises over 50%, exceeds 256 micromol/L or eGFR is about 20-25, stop if hypovolaemic; if any uncertainty, seek specialist advice urgently.

src.q: Serum creatinine level increase of 30 to 50%, or value greater than 200 micromol/L, or eGFR less than 30 mL/min/1.73 m2 Ensure prompt clinical review of volume status. Reduce dose or stop if patient hypovolaemic. Re-measure renal function within 1 week.
Serum creatinine level increase of more than 50%, or value greater than 256 micromol/L, or eGFR approximately 20 to 25 mL/min/1.73 m2
Assess volume status and respond: if patient hypovolaemic, stop furosemide
If any uncertainty, seek specialist advice urgently.

items.t: Contraindicated in pre-coma/coma with hepatic cirrhosis or encephalopathy. Caution in impaired hepatic function (monitoring required); dose adjustment may be needed in liver congestion. Hepatic encephalopathy may occur in hepatocellular insufficiency.

Impaired hepatic function (see sections 4.2 and 4.3 and below - monitoring required)

items.t: One UK SmPC: crosses the placenta; must not be given in pregnancy unless there are compelling medical reasons; monitor fetal growth.

src.q: It must not be given during pregnancy unless there are compelling medical reasons. Treatment during pregnancy requires monitoring of fetal growth.
however, furosemide crosses the placental barrier

items.t: Another UK SmPC: should not be used in pregnancy unless benefits outweigh the possible fetal risk (including persistent patent ductus arteriosus).

src.q: The drug should not be used in pregnant women unless the benefits to the patient outweigh the possible risk to the foetus which includes persistence of patent ductus arteriosus

items.t: BUMPS (diuretics): can be used in pregnancy if prescribed but rarely needed; may reduce blood flow to the placenta (extra growth scans). In heart failure a diuretic may need to continue.

src.q: A diuretic can be used in pregnancy if prescribed by a doctor.
if you are using a diuretic because you have heart failure, you may be advised to continue taking a diuretic
Diuretics can be used in pregnancy but are rarely needed.
Diuretics may reduce blood flow to the placenta.
Your baby will be monitored with extra growth scans.

items.t: Contraindicated in breastfeeding women (section 4.3 of both UK SmPCs). Passes into milk and may inhibit lactation; one SmPC says women must not breastfeed during treatment.

src.q: Breast-feeding women (see section 4.6)
Furosemide passes into breast milk and may inhibit lactation. Women must not breastfeed if they are treated with furosemide.

items.t: Conflict: section 4.6 of the other UK SmPC says use with caution in nursing mothers, while its section 4.3 lists breastfeeding as a contraindication.

src.q: Furosemide may pass into the breast milk or may inhibit lactation, it should therefore be used with caution in nursing mothers.

items.t: No human data on fertility.

src.q: No human data on the effect of furosemide on fertility are available.

items.t: Severe anaphylactic or anaphylactoid reactions with shock (rare); serious skin reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome, Lyell's syndrome, AGEP, DRESS) - one SmPC says withdraw treatment if skin reactions occur; interstitial nephritis and acute renal failure (rare); acute pancreatitis (rare).

src.q: Rare: Severe anaphylactic or anaphylactoid reactions (e.g. with shock) occur rarely

exsudative erythema multiforme (Lyell's syndrome and Stevens-Johnson syndrome)

items.t: Oral; usually in the morning (diuresis lasts about 4 hours, so timing can suit the patient). Take bile acid sequestrants 2-3 hours apart and sucralfate at least 2 hours apart.

src.q: Diuresis lasts for approximately four hours following administration and hence the time of administration can be adjusted to suit the patient's requirements.

items.t: If diarrhoea and vomiting develop, keep drinking and stop furosemide for 1-2 days until recovered; have renal function checked if symptoms last beyond 2 days (SPS).

src.q: If patients develop diarrhoea and vomiting while on furosemide treatment, they should maintain their fluid intake and stop furosemide for 1 to 2 days until they recover.
